extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and patent-office practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing U.S. patent-office procedure: role and limits of the Commissioner and examiners; the nature, content, duration, and effect of caveats; attorney appointment, authority, duties, fees, and discipline; and when patent privilege vests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's ministerial jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner is a ministerial officer with jurisdiction over the whole matter of examination of applications and the grant and issue of patents, but in discharging these ministerial duties he is subject to the statutes and the rules of the Office; his powers cannot be extended beyond these either by his own authority or by construction of the courts. The Acting Commissioner is, for all legal purposes, the Commissioner; his jurisdiction cannot be collaterally attacked and patents certified and allowed by him are of the same validity as those issued by the Commissioner in person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases (e.g., Stone v. Greaves, Dorsey Harvester Rake Co. v. Marsh). The Office's written rules and statutes limit the Commissioner's powers; ministerial (not judicial) character of functions emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners' duties and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners (except Examiners-in-Chief) are appointed by the Commissioner and charged with duties including correcting errors in descriptions of alleged inventions in applications, examining the novelty and utility of such inventions, and hearing and deciding upon the claims of rival inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners cannot pass on matters expressly decided by a superior tribunal; their jurisdiction does not change with the person occupying the office; proceedings of the Patent Office are presumed regular. See Ex parte Reynolds, Ex parte Fredericks, and related citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent applications — objects and required oath
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant must file in the Patent Office an application describing and claiming a patentable invention resulting from his own creative act and must support his application by an oath that he believes himself the first and true inventor of the art or instrument therein described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examination finds allegations correct, petition is formally allowed and letters-patent issued. Primary objects: (1) secure exclusive privilege; (2) prevent a similar grant to a rival. References to later discussion of description, claims, drawings, fees, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent privilege vests only on issuance of letters-patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The final action creating the patent privilege is the issuance of the letters-patent; neither application nor admission of novelty/utility by examiners nor favorable decisions in contests establishes rights against the public — only the actual issue does so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mode of issue, form and contents of instrument, term of monopoly, and acts to be performed by inventor upon receiving notice are specifically prescribed by law. Cite §§617–682 for further rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat purpose — priority protection (general nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat is intended to secure to an inventor the opportunity to have the question of priority between himself and a rival determined before the issue of letters-patent to either; it is a written notice that the caveator claims to be the first and true inventor of the art or instrument described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its effect is to entitle the caveator to notice of subsequent applications for the same subject matter; it does not protect against public use, does not substitute for due diligence in perfecting/reducing invention to practice, and gives no substantive advantage over rivals other than the notice right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may file a caveat (eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a U.S. citizen or an alien who has resided in the U.S. for one year preceding filing and has formally declared intent to become a citizen may file a caveat; the filer must be the actual inventor and must believe himself to be the first inventor, and must desire further time to mature his invention before applying for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat cannot be used to reserve rights when inventor allows invention to go into public use; some subject-matter (e.g., immature designs) cannot properly be caveated until complete enough to be patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents of a caveat (formal requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat must consist of a petition on oath, a specification, and in some cases a drawing. The petition alleges citizenship or resident alienage, the inventive act, and desire to perfect invention; oath affirms these; specification describes the object of invention and its distinguishing characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification need not be as particular as a patent application but must be complete and exact enough to enable examiners to determine whether a later application probably describes the same invention. Caveat must be limited to one invention; amendments describing different or additional inventions require separate caveats. When practicable include a full and accurate drawing folded for filing. The caveat must be signed by the inventor (one signature suffices for joint inventions) and accompanied by the established fee; failure to comply renders caveat invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing and secrecy of caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: On receipt in proper form, the caveat is filed in the secret archives of the Office and remains during its life inaccessible except to the inventor, his authorized agent, and officers of the department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No information as to existence or contents may be given to others unless directed by the caveator. Fraudulent disclosure of a caveat to a rival does not bar the rival from obtaining a patent for the invention described if his application was filed prior to the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and renewal of caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat remains in force for one year from date of its acceptance by the Patent Office and may be renewed for successive years by payment of additional fee; if not renewed it remains in secret archives but ceases to secure rights to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewal is by payment; the caveat's practical protection (notice rights) lapses if not kept in force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and procedure upon subsequent applications (suspension and interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a rival files an application during the life of a caveat and the Office finds the described invention patentable and apparently corresponding to that in the caveat, proceedings on the application are suspended, the rival application is deposited in secret archives, and the caveator is notified to file his application so claims can be determined; if both applications claim the same invention an interference will be declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The caveator must present his application within three months from the expiration of ordinary mail transmission time for the notice from Washington. If the Office or mail fails to give notice and a patent issues, the patentee cannot take advantage of that patent in later interference between him and the caveator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent attorneys — choice, supervision, and qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor may choose any person of intelligence and good moral character to act as his attorney in patent prosecution. All such attorneys act under the supervision of the Commissioner and are subject to withdrawal of privileges for misconduct. Patent attorneys are not required to be learned lawyers and are not agents of the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No special privileges permitted to any attorney over another; relative facility in procuring patents depends on individual diligence and skill. Rules governing conduct derive from Office regulations and ordinary law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment by written power of attorney (formalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney can be appointed only by a written power of attorney, and the Patent Office does not recognize the attorney until the power has been duly filed. The written power must be signed by the inventor/applicant and must name each and every person upon whom the attorneyship is to be conferred; a power given to a firm must specifically mention each member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A power may contain written authorization allowing the original attorney to substitute or associate another, but such substitute/associate cannot delegate his authority further. Even members of Congress must file written power before acting in patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of attorney limited to the application accompanying the power
rubrics_metrics.description: The relation created by filing a written power of attorney refers only to the particular proceedings of which the power forms a part and ends when that proceeding is concluded; if several applications are instituted concurrently, a separate power must be filed in each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For certain notice purposes the Office may continue to recognize an attorney as a medium of communication after the business is completed. Associate attorney appointment practices and requirements apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocability and revocation of power of attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: A power of attorney may be irrevocable when it constitutes part of a contract conferring a beneficial interest on the attorney; otherwise it is revocable at the client's pleasure. Revocation should be given in writing to the Patent Office, which will notify the attorney and thereafter deal with the client or his new attorney.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Death of the principal also terminates a revocable power; assignment of an undivided interest does not revoke a prior power; where a power was conferred before assignment of entire interest, authority of the attorney of the assignor expires and a new appointment or ratification is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney as sole medium of communication and duties of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: After filing of the power, all correspondence between the Office and the inventor takes place through his attorney. The attorney has a right to inspect papers in the case and consult with examiners, and must conduct himself with courtesy and decorum; disrespectful or improper written submissions will ordinarily be returned without action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dealings with client, attorney is subject to general agency rules and must use such skill and diligence as the business demands. The culpable neglect or fraud of an attorney will not prejudice the principal unless instigated or accepted by the principal or unless public interests or vested rights would be unjustly violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation and lien of patent attorneys
rubrics_metrics.description: The attorney has a lien upon the papers of his client for his fees. The letters-patent, when issued, are delivered to him if he so desires and may be retained until his reasonable charges for services and disbursements have been paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associate or substitute attorneys have similar privileges with respect to papers that come into their possession, though the patent itself will not be delivered by the Office without a special order from the primary attorney.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to suspend or disbar attorneys for cause
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner may suspend or dismiss attorneys for gross misconduct toward the Patent Office or their clients; this statutory power is exercised frequently and may be general or particular in scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hearing upon formal charges is accorded; any order for dismissal and its reasons must be submitted to and approved by the Secretary of the Interior before taking effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office practice shaped by statutes, rules, and established usage
rubrics_metrics.description: In conducting proceedings the Patent Office is guided by acts of Congress, written Office rules, and its own established practice. Statutes and rules receive practical interpretation by application to particular facts, and methods of procedure are extended or defined by usages subordinate to written law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the Commissioner's powers to formalize usages, there is less room for purely traditional regulations in the Patent Office than in many other tribunals; references to earlier/later sections for particular practices (e.g., §§ 451–487).

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters-patent by special act of Congress (exceptional grants)
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain cases letters-patent may be granted without intervention of the Patent Office by special act of Congress to secure exclusive use to an inventor whose case is not within the Office's statutory jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such patents fall under general provisions of law except when otherwise specified by the act; Congress' constitutional power to grant such monopolies is broad, but existing monopolies cannot be abrogated or curtailed by the manner of the grant.
